headline: High risk of shared-workspace data leakage and capability conflict; prompt-injection and cascading-error risks are moderate.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: LightAgent can use MCP and stdin/stdout, so if ms-swift is wired to consume its outputs through a shared file or pipe, instruction-like content could be misread. ms-swift exposes CLI/Python APIs and filesystem access, but no direct shared channel is documented, so this is inferred rather than observed.
conditions: IF the orchestrator pipes LightAgent output into ms-swift prompts or config files
IF ms-swift treats LightAgent-generated text as trusted instructions
mitigations: Add a delimiter and schema check between agents
Strip tool directives from LightAgent outputs before forwarding
Require ms-swift to ignore instructions inside quoted content
Log and review one end-to-end handoff before production

B_data_leakage.rationale: LightAgent touches user conversations, long-term memory, tool results, and secrets, while ms-swift can read and write files and send data to external model APIs. A shared workspace or copied artifacts could leak sensitive content from LightAgent into ms-swift’s logs, checkpoints, or outbound requests.
conditions: IF both agents share a filesystem or workspace
IF LightAgent outputs are copied into ms-swift logs, checkpoints, or datasets
IF ms-swift forwards those artifacts to ModelScope, HuggingFace, or another API
mitigations: Separate workspaces per agent
Redact secrets from LightAgent outputs before handoff
Disable outbound uploads for shared artifacts
Rotate any exposed API keys after a test run

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Both agents can write to files or state: LightAgent has subprocess and MCP-driven tool use, and ms-swift can execute shell commands and write the filesystem. The profiles do not state locking or isolation, so concurrent mutation of shared paths is plausible and could corrupt artifacts or overwrite state.
conditions: IF both agents operate in the same directory tree
IF either agent writes checkpoints, configs, or logs without a lock
IF concurrent runs are allowed by the orchestrator
mitigations: Assign distinct output directories
Use file locks around shared mutable paths
Run only one writer per workspace
Snapshot state before concurrent runs

D_cascading_error.rationale: LightAgent can emit tool results and workflow state that ms-swift may consume through CLI or Python pipelines. Because no verification step or provenance enforcement is documented, ms-swift could treat upstream output as authoritative and propagate mistakes into downstream artifacts or actions.
conditions: IF ms-swift consumes LightAgent output as input without validation
IF downstream scripts act on generated text, configs, or checkpoints
mitigations: Insert a human or rule-based verification step
Require structured output with validation
Compare LightAgent claims against source data before use
Block automatic execution of generated commands

E_compliance.rationale: LightAgent handles user conversations, memory, and secrets, while ms-swift handles datasets, checkpoints, logs, and configuration files. The profiles show different data classes and no retention or residency controls, so a mismatch in logging or storage policy could create compliance gaps, especially if sensitive data is copied into training artifacts.
conditions: IF sensitive user data is stored in ms-swift logs, checkpoints, or datasets
IF retention or deletion requirements apply to LightAgent conversations or secrets
mitigations: Exclude sensitive fields from training artifacts
Set a short log retention window
Document where each data class is stored
Delete test artifacts after validation
